Female Knight Gobies attain a maximum total length of approximately 6.4 centimeters [Li = approximately 6.4 centimeters], a modest size typical of many species within the family Gobiidae. Growth trajectories in this species appear strongly influenced by local thermal conditions, with individuals reared at a stable water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C] reaching sexual maturity upon achieving a total length of 4.1 centimeters [Lp = 4.1 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet body mass of roughly 0.71 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.71 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of individuals from brackish estuarine habitats. The relationship between length and mass is relatively consistent across populations, though slight variations have been noted in specimens collected from more saline environments. Field surveys indicate that the transition from juvenile to mature body sizes occurs over a period of several months, depending on local resource availability and temperature regimes. The ultimate size of 6.4 centimeters [Li = 6.4 centimeters] is rarely exceeded in wild populations, suggesting an asymptotic growth pattern consistent with determinate growth models documented in other small-bodied, iteroparous gobies.

The incubation period for the embryonic stage is remarkably brief under controlled conditions. At a water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], embryos complete development and the fertilized ova hatch after just 7 days [ab = 7 days]. This rapid eclosion is characteristic of tropical and subtropical gobiid species that deposit small, adhesive demersal eggs in sheltered microhabitats such as empty bivalve shells or under rock crevices. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minuscule, with a wet weight at birth of merely 0.000065 grams [Wwb = 0.000065 grams], reflecting the diminutive size of the egg, which measures approximately 0.5 millimeters in diameter. This extraordinarily low mass at hamming imposes a stringent energetic constraint on the prolarva, which must rely entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. The lecithotrophic phase is consequently short, typically lasting only a few days before the mouth opens and the larva must successfully capture its first prey to avoid starvation.

Reproductive output in the Knight Goby is characterized by a relatively high fecundity combined with modest individual egg size. Females produce clutches averaging approximately 15 to 16 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 15 to 16 eggs per spawning event] and can complete a single reproductive cycle each day under optimal conditions [F_R_i = single reproductive cycle each day under optimal conditions] at a stable water temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C]. This daily spawning frequency translates to a daily reproduction rate of approximately 15 to 16 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 15 to 16 eggs per day], a value that is unusual among fishes of comparable body size and suggests a remarkable capacity for rapid oocyte recruitment and vitellogenesis. The ability to sustain such a high reproductive rate implies substantial energetic investment and likely depends on a continuous, abundant supply of small invertebrate prey. The combination of a moderate clutch size and an exceptionally short inter-spawning interval results in a very high lifetime reproductive output, although individual fecundity may decline as females approach the end of their reproductive lifespan. Such a strategy is typical of species that experience high, unpredictable juvenile mortality and compensate through sheer numbers of offspring.

The asymptotic wet mass of adult females, based on the length-weight relationship established for this species, reaches approximately 2.76 grams [Wwi = approximately 2.76 grams]. This ultimate body mass is congruent with the maximum recorded total length of 6.4 centimeters [Li = 6.4 centimeters] and is consistent across multiple estuarine populations sampled throughout the species' range. In comparison, the wet mass at puberty, roughly 0.71 grams [Wwp = roughly 0.71 grams], represents only about 26% of the ultimate adult mass, indicating that females invest a substantial portion of their somatic growth after the onset of reproductive activity. This pattern of early maturation at a relatively small size, followed by continued body mass increase, is common among small, short-lived teleosts that face intense predation pressure. The post-pubertal growth increment is presumably fueled by efficient foraging on benthic microcrustaceans and insect larvae. The length-weight coefficient for the species has a value of 0.00977, with an exponent of 3.04, closely approximating the cube law expected for isometric growth in fishes.

Lifespan in the Knight Goby is remarkably constrained under natural conditions. At the standard reference temperature of 17.1 °C [T = 17.1 °C], the maximum documented longevity is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], with very few individuals surviving beyond 36 months in either wild or captive settings. This short lifespan places the species firmly within the category of annual or near-annual fishes, a life-history strategy that is often associated with high early mortality and intense reproductive effort concentrated into a single breeding season. Senescence appears to set in rapidly after the first year of life, with noticeable declines in body condition, feeding activity, and spawning frequency observed in older individuals. Comparative data from closely related congeneric species suggest that even slight increases in average water temperature, within the species' thermal tolerance range, can further accelerate the physiological aging process, reducing the already brief lifespan. The combination of early maturity, extremely high daily reproductive output, and short adult survival defines a life-history strategy heavily skewed toward rapid population turnover.
